name: Olga Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Birchwood Timber Homes, a small country builder that puts up timber houses, mostly for farmers' children and people moving out from the city. I split my time between the joinery workshop, where I make stairs and window frames, and the sites, where we fit them. Last year the boss bought a computer-controlled cutting machine for the stair parts, and I learned it after the foreman had worked the bugs out. I like the smell of the workshop in the morning and a staircase that doesn't creak. What wears me out is driving forty minutes on gravel roads to a site and then finding the delivery hasn't come.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Erik last year, he's a mechanic who fixes farm machinery, tractors and combines mostly. We rent a cottage near his parents' farm and we're saving for our own place, but honestly we've got less than a month put by after the wedding. Birchwood pays a bit under the city firms, and out here there aren't many building jobs at all. I use AI now and then, mostly to help price the dining tables I make at weekends and sell online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's fine by me. We've got enough to worry about out here without that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy calculator. At church or at the feed store, people would nod. I might post a picture of a table I made by hand with a line about it, people like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means our plans stay on track: save for a house, have children in a couple of years, keep working at Birchwood. That's what I want. If AI just helps me price my tables, that's useful and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. Work at Birchwood, sell more tables at weekends, put the table money straight into the house fund. Maybe ask the boss about more hours in the workshop over winter, when sites are slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many tables do you sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One or two a month, from oak or ash I get from a sawmill down the valley. It's maybe a fifth of what I earn at Birchwood, which isn't nothing. Erik helps with the finishing when he's not fixing someone's tractor at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house you're saving for look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A timber house, obviously, one I'd build half of myself. Two bedrooms, a workshop out the back, near Erik's parents. His mum already talks about babysitting, and we haven't even started trying.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy calculator. People at church or the feed store would nod, and I might post a photo of a handmade table with a line about it.
S0.think: Privately it means our plans stay on track: save for a house, have children in a couple of years and keep working at Birchwood. If AI just helps me price tables, that's enough.
S0.do: Keeps working at Birchwood, sells more weekend tables and puts that money straight into the house fund. Asks for more workshop hours over winter.
S0.quote: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy calculator.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is rooted in a rural community with clear plans for a house and children. She already has a small side income from handmade tables and uses AI only to price them. She adopted the workshop's cutting machine once the foreman had proved it, a sign of her steady approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to what I see coming. We've already got one machine in the workshop, so I know how this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses that adapt will be fine and people should learn new skills instead of waiting for someone to save them. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever. I'd say it at church and to the young lads at Birchwood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the workshop would change first. The cutting machine already does in an hour what took me a day on stair strings, the side pieces that hold the steps. More machines like that and Birchwood needs fewer people in the shop, and I'm in the shop half the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the next machine the boss buys, after the foreman, same as last time. I'd use AI more for my table business, for designs and pricing, and try to sell three a month instead of one or two. I'd keep saving, but I'd want that side business ready in case my hours went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if Birchwood cut people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. A business has to stay alive, and if the boss doesn't buy machines, the bigger firms will undercut him and we'd all lose. I'd rather he buys the machine and keeps some of us than goes under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young lads at Birchwood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machine, and learn the old way too. When the machine breaks, which it does, somebody has to know how to cut a stair string by hand. That somebody keeps their job.

S1.say: I'd say businesses that adapt will be fine and people should learn new skills instead of waiting to be saved. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever, at church and to the young workers at Birchwood.
S1.think: Privately I think the workshop would change first, since the cutting machine already does in an hour what took me a day. More machines means fewer people in the shop, and I'm there half the week.
S1.do: Learns the next machine after the foreman, as before, and uses AI more for designing and pricing her tables. Aims to sell three tables a month and builds the side business as a backup while saving.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching closely but not frightened.
S1.quote: When the machine breaks, which it does, somebody has to know how to cut a stair string by hand.
S1.fieldNote: Olga doesn't blame her boss for buying machines, seeing it as the price of the firm surviving. She has a concrete backup plan in her table business. Her advice to young workers, learn the machine and the old way, shows her practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. With robots too. That's a lot. I'd need to sit down and think about that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because we can't just wait for a cheque from the government. I'd say it at church, and I think people would be scared and need someone calm. I'd try to be that, even if I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think Birchwood would close, or keep one person to watch the machines. And who buys a handmade table when nobody has a job? Erik's work fixing farm machines might last a bit longer, but they'd have robots for that too in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Erik we wait on children, which would break my heart a bit. We'd cut everything back, stop the house fund and just keep the rent paid. We'd lean on his parents, maybe move into the old farmhouse cottage with them, and I'd sell what tables I could to anyone still buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake next to Erik, doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to be the calm one at church. Would that be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. But my grandmother did it when the mill closed in her town, she made soup for half the street and never once let anyone see her cry. I'd want to be like her. I'd cry in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was there and we needed it, I'd take it, but I'd feel ashamed doing it. I'd rather it came as work, building things, than as money for nothing. Maybe that's old-fashioned.

S2.say: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because we can't just wait for a government cheque. I'd say it at church and try to be the calm one, even if I wasn't.
S2.think: Privately I think Birchwood would close or keep one person to watch the machines. Nobody buys handmade tables when nobody has a job, and robots would reach Erik's farm machinery work in the end too.
S2.do: Puts off having children, stops the house fund and keeps only the rent paid. Leans on Erik's parents, possibly moving into the farmhouse cottage, and sells tables to anyone still buying.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums in her head.
S2.quote: I'd want to be like her. I'd cry in the truck.
S2.fieldNote: Olga's response is about family and community, modelled on a grandmother who held a street together when a mill closed. Delaying children is the hardest cost for her. She would accept government help only with shame and would much rather it came as work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but it's not nothing. We could plan around five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so people should get practical: learn what they can, save what they can, look after their neighbours. I'd say businesses should train people, not just buy machines. And I'd say it without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes me think hard about children. Do we have them now, so they're little while we still have work, or do we wait? I'd probably say now, honestly. Better to be a young mother with a job than wait and have neither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Erik about starting a family in the next year rather than in two. I'd keep working at Birchwood and save hard, and I'd grow the table business, maybe add bespoke stairs for people restoring old houses, because rich people might still pay for handmade. I'd learn the AI tools better, for the selling side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. In control, mostly, but there's a clock ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's the opposite of what you said with two years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years there's no time to get on our feet. With five, a baby would be at school before things get really bad, and we'd have a few years of two wages first. It's about the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, Erik's old pickup, we'd share mine. Eating out, which is rare anyway. Maybe the new table saw I've been wanting, which hurts.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so people should get practical: learn and save what they can and look after their neighbours. I'd say businesses should train people, not just buy machines, and I'd say it without panic.
S3.think: Privately five years makes me think hard about children, and I'd probably say have them now. Better to be a young mother with a job than wait and have neither.
S3.do: Talks to Erik about starting a family within a year, keeps working at Birchwood and saves hard by dropping the second car. Grows the table business into bespoke stairs for old houses and learns AI tools for selling.
S3.feel: Anxious but mostly in control, with a clock ticking.
S3.quote: Better to be a young mother with a job than wait and have neither.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips Olga's family plan: she'd bring children forward rather than delay them, and she explains the timing herself. Her side business shifts towards high-end handmade work for people who might still pay. She remains steady, adopting AI for selling rather than for her craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a proper stretch of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people who are willing to work and learn. I'd say communities and churches should be helping young families plan. I'd be fairly calm saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. We'd have children and maybe our own house before it lands. Birchwood might not last, but I could build up the table and stair business by then, enough to live on, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Birchwood, have children on our normal plan, and save for the house. I'd build the furniture business slowly, a few more pieces each year, and use AI tools for the website and the selling. I'd watch the workshop machines closely and learn each one once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of worry at the back, but mostly I'd feel like we had time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really think handmade furniture survives when robots can make anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes. People still buy hand-thrown pottery even though factories make cups for almost nothing. It won't be a big business. It might be enough for one woman and her husband's tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two we'd wait on children and live with his parents. With ten we'd have a family and a house of our own, I hope. It's the difference between starting our life and putting it on hold.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for people willing to work and learn, and that communities and churches should help young families plan. I'd say it fairly calmly.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable, with children and maybe our own house before it lands. Birchwood might not last, but I could build the table and stair business into something to live on, maybe.
S4.do: Keeps working at Birchwood, has children on the normal timeline and saves for a house. Grows the furniture business a little each year, uses AI for the website and sales, and learns new workshop machines once proven.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, but mostly feels there's time.
S4.quote: It might be enough for one woman and her husband's tractors.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Olga keep her family plan unchanged and slowly grow a handmade furniture business she believes will survive in a small way. She compares it to handmade pottery. The contrast she draws is between starting life and putting it on hold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Erik and I would have to put our whole life on hold, children and house both. What would help is work, real work, maybe building things communities need, and apprenticeships for whatever comes next. And customers who still value something made by hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the country. Out here we're forty minutes from anything. When a job goes in the city, there's another down the road. When Birchwood goes, there's nothing for fifty miles. People forget that.

headlineQuote: When Birchwood goes, there's nothing for fifty miles.
portrait: Olga Olsen is a 27-year-old joiner at a small country timber-house builder, splitting her time between the workshop and sites, newly married to Erik, a farm machinery mechanic, with less than a month of savings after the wedding. She uses AI now and then to price the dining tables she sells at weekends, and learns new workshop machines once they're proven. She is content with the plateau and uneasy about steady disruption, where her side business is the backup. AGI in two years alarms her and would mean putting off children, while with five years she'd have them sooner and with ten keep her plans as they are.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Erik would have to put both children and a house on hold.
whatWouldHelp: Real work, such as building things communities need, apprenticeships for what comes next, and customers who still value handmade work.
